capability_summary: The single authoritative definition of CircleTel's visual identity — the logo system (eight named variants, anatomy, variant-selection rules, clearspace, minimum sizes, and the absolute prohibition on a generative model drawing the mark), the colour palette with exact hex values and their permitted and prohibited roles, the typography stack and scale, and the brand's tone and South African market context. It serves these facts on demand to every consumer that renders something CircleTel-branded: AI image generation, web and admin UI code, print and large-format, email, social avatars, sales collateral, decks and product documentation. It states values exactly rather than by name, resolves which logo variant is correct for a given background and medium, discloses rather than silently resolves conflicts between the repository's brand sources, and labels any derived answer as a derivation rather than an established rule.
user_goal: Stop CircleTel work being off-brand or inconsistently branded. The user wants one place to ask 'what is CircleTel's orange / heading font / logo for a dark background / clearspace' and get an exact, correct, reusable answer — so that an image, a web page, a deck and a printed banner produced months apart by different agents and tools look like the same company. Secondarily and specifically: the user wants the brand rendered correctly by machines that cannot be trusted to draw it, which is why exact hex values are mandated over colour names and why the real logo files are composited in rather than imitated by a model.
success_looks_like: Asked for a brand value, the capability returns an exact hex (and RGB where a print or non-CSS medium needs it) together with the source or token that value belongs to and where it may and may not be used — never the bare word 'orange'.

The values it states match the values the production design tokens actually define; a divergence between the guideline and the shipped product is a failure of this capability, not an acceptable variance.
Every hex it quotes alongside a design-token name resolves to that hex in tailwind.config.ts; a token/hex mismatch is a defect.
Asked which logo to use, it names one specific variant from the eight-file set and gives the reason (background luminance, medium, size), rather than handing back the whole table.

The CircleTel logo in any produced asset is the real logo artwork, pixel-identical to the file in .design/logos/ — never a generative model's redrawing of it. Artwork is generated logo-free with space reserved, then the real file is composited on.
Clearspace and minimum size are respected, so the mark is never crowded or reproduced below legibility.
Asset dimensions and aspect ratio match the destination on the first attempt, so nothing is cropped, letterboxed or upscaled later.
The same brand fact requested through different consumers — image prompt, React component, print spec, deck, product document — yields the same value, with no consumer-specific drift.
The visual register is consistently modern, clean, professional, trustworthy, innovative and approachable — no clip-art, no neon, no busy compositions, no off-brand colours.
People, settings and props read as authentically South African wherever an asset depicts human or lifestyle context.
When two repository sources disagree on a brand fact, the capability surfaces the conflict with both values and their provenance instead of quietly asserting one.

Asked for a brand decision the definition does not cover, it produces a derivation grounded in the stated palette roles and hierarchy, says plainly that it is a derivation rather than an established rule, and states what would make it official — it neither invents silently nor refuses.
The user is told which brand decisions were made on their behalf (which variant, which ratio, which orange), so the output is auditable and correctable.
A finished asset is verified against the brand before it is handed over, and lands in a predictable categorised location rather than scattered.
A second person picking up the same brand facts months later produces an asset that sits beside the earlier one without a visible mismatch.

priority_qualities.quality: Factual exactness of brand values, and their agreement with the production design tokens
priority_qualities.why_it_matters: This capability exists to be the source of truth. A wrong hex, a wrong typeface or a wrong token mapping propagates silently into shipped pages, printed banners and paid ad creative, and is expensive to unwind. It is also the capability's live failure mode: six of its core facts currently disagree with what production ships, and its Tailwind mapping is factually false against the config. Exactness beats completeness, coverage and prose quality; every other quality is downstream of the numbers being right.

priority_qualities.quality: Logo integrity — the mark is always the real asset file, never generated, redrawn, distorted or approximated
priority_qualities.why_it_matters: The logo is a registered mark with legal and recognition value, and the one asset that must never be approximated. Generative models reliably mangle the swirl geometry and the wordmark. A plausible-looking generated imitation is a worse failure than a missing logo because it ships unnoticed, looks amateurish or fraudulent, and can erode trademark distinctiveness. Every other brand error is a matter of degree; this one makes the asset unusable.

priority_qualities.quality: Single source of truth — the thing others reference, not another copy
priority_qualities.why_it_matters: Brand facts are currently restated independently in at least nine places (this skill, its quick-reference, DESIGN.md, tailwind.config.ts, app/globals.css and six sibling generation skills), and they have already drifted apart. Every extra copy is a future inconsistency. Correcting the values here without fixing the propagation model just makes them stale again in three months.

priority_qualities.quality: Consumer-neutrality — answers for web UI, print, email, social, collateral and image generation alike
priority_qualities.why_it_matters: Framing the brand only in image-prompt terms forces every other consumer to write its own copy, which is exactly how the current drift happened. Three non-image skills already declare a dependency on this capability, so the demand is demonstrably broader than the framing it was given.

priority_qualities.quality: Automatic application at the point of use, without having to be asked
priority_qualities.why_it_matters: Documented brand rules that must be consciously recalled are the rules that get skipped on the 'quick one'. The value is that guidance fires on every brand-relevant request, including small, internal, draft and urgent ones. If it only applies when explicitly invoked, drift resumes immediately.

priority_qualities.quality: Correct variant and contrast selection for the actual background
priority_qualities.why_it_matters: A dark mark on a dark field, or an orange mark over an orange gradient, is invisible; a technically on-brand asset whose logo cannot be read is a failed asset. The reason eight variants exist is so the right one is chosen automatically rather than debated each time.

A brand guide that returns a table and no answer forces the caller to guess, reintroducing the inconsistency it exists to prevent. It must pick — and be explicit about whether the pick is an established rule, a derivation, or a contested value with a pending human decision.

priority_qualities.quality: Fit-for-destination output — aspect ratio, resolution, format and file placement
priority_qualities.why_it_matters: Wrong ratio means the platform crops the logo or the price callout; wrong resolution fails in print. Cheap to get right up front, expensive to fix once the asset is live or printed.

priority_qualities.quality: Consistent aesthetic register and restraint over decoration
priority_qualities.why_it_matters: Matching hex codes do not by themselves make a coherent brand; a set of images varying wildly in style still reads as inconsistent. The brand's promise is trustworthiness in a market where ISPs are widely distrusted, and busy, neon or clip-art visuals actively undercut the commercial message.

Generic imported stock imagery signals 'not for you' to the actual customer base and reads as a foreign brand rather than a local operator, undermining the local-and-trustworthy positioning the brand is built on.

priority_qualities.quality: Verifiability of the finished artefact before release
priority_qualities.why_it_matters: The user wants errors caught in-house rather than by a customer seeing the wrong orange. This is weaker than it looks today: the check is made by eye, and generative models reliably drift orange toward yellow or gold, so a real measurement against the approved hex is the missing mechanism.

Values are consumed by machines and by people mid-task; formats that paste straight into a prompt, a stylesheet or a print spec remove a whole class of transcription errors. Assets that cannot be found get regenerated with drift, so a stable categorised location is what keeps a set of assets looking like a set.

constraints: Colours must be expressed as exact hex values, and as RGB where a print or non-CSS medium needs it — never as a colour name alone.
Every colour must carry its permitted role and its prohibited roles; a value without a usage rule invites misuse.
Where a design-token name is quoted alongside a hex, the token must actually resolve to that hex in tailwind.config.ts. The config is authoritative over any prose restatement of a token.
Where the repository's brand sources disagree on a fact, the disagreement must be reported with both values and their provenance, not silently resolved.
The logo is only ever supplied by referencing the real artwork in .design/logos/. The eight variants are a fixed, named set and any selection must resolve to exactly one of them.

Logo variant must be chosen by background luminance, medium and size using the documented selection rules — including a stated fallback for visually noisy backgrounds (quiet region, scrim/plate, or the self-backgrounded orange-square lockup).
Clearspace equal to the height of the 'TEL' wordmark element must be maintained on all sides.
The logo must never be reproduced below 32px height for digital or 10mm height for print.
Generated imagery must be produced deliberately without the logo, with space reserved for it, and the real logo composited afterwards.
Output aspect ratio and resolution must be selected to match the asset's destination before generating.
Aesthetic register is fixed: modern, clean, professional, uncluttered, trustworthy, innovative, approachable — not neon, not busy, not clip-art, not generic Western stock.

South African market context governs people, settings, props, language and cultural cues in any depictive asset, operationalised concretely (realistic demographic mix, plausible local settings, local vehicles/signage/plug types) rather than asserted as a slogan.

Accessibility is a brand constraint, not a separate concern: colour must never be the sole carrier of meaning, and orange used as text on light backgrounds must use the accessible variant rather than the primary.
Typography in generated imagery must be consistent with the brand's shipped typefaces rather than left as an unnamed 'clean sans-serif'.

Any price, speed, coverage or contractual claim rendered into an image must be verified against the current live offer, be legible at thumbnail size, and carry whatever qualifier the offer requires — or be overlaid as real text rather than generated.

Third-party and partner logos are outside the CircleTel brand definition and are governed by the icon and licensing rules (licence check, trademark check, local hosting for production-critical use, accessible naming).
Interface iconography is Phosphor-based and is not a free design choice within branded UI; brand-driven styling must not override that system.
Generated assets must be filed into the designated categorised output tree, not left loose or in the project root, and never overwrite the authoritative logo files.
A pre-release verification must be performed and its outcome stated before an asset is considered finished.
The brand decisions made on the user's behalf (variant chosen, ratio chosen, which orange lineage applied) must be stated back to the user.
never_do: Never ask a generative model to draw, render, recreate, approximate or 'faithfully reproduce' the CircleTel logo, wordmark or swirl mark.
Never specify a brand colour by name only ('orange', 'navy', 'the brand blue') where a hex value exists.
Never quote a design-token name alongside a hex without having confirmed the token actually holds that hex.
Never present a contested brand value as settled, or silently pick one side of a documented conflict.
Never silently invent a brand rule to fill a gap and present it as established.
Never answer a brand question with only a table and no recommendation.
Never emit a colour outside the approved palette as a brand colour, and never introduce a new brand colour without flagging it as unofficial.
Never repurpose a reserved colour for an unrelated purpose — the semantic success/error/info colours, and the WhatsApp green which is exclusive to the WhatsApp CTA.
Never place a logo variant on a background it was not made for — a light-background lockup on dark, a dark or grey lockup over orange, or a coloured variant over a busy photograph without a plate.
Never distort, recolour, rotate, stretch, crop into, add effects to, or re-typeset the logo, and never normalise the wordmark casing.
Never violate clearspace or reproduce the logo below the stated minimum size.
Never skip brand context on the grounds that an image is quick, internal, exploratory or a draft.
Never produce clip-art, cartoonish, neon or visually busy compositions.
Never let one consumer — image generation — define the brand for all the others.
Never let generated imagery imply a partnership, endorsement, coverage claim, product capability, price or performance figure that is not true.
Never depict a third party's trademark, product or network branding inside CircleTel artwork without an authorised reason.
Never ship a third-party or provider logo without confirming its licence, attribution and trademark position.
Never save assets outside the agreed folder structure or overwrite the authoritative logo source files.
Never publish an asset without the pre-release brand verification having been run.
objective_invariants: TOKEN AGREEMENT (the governing invariant) — every colour hex this capability states, together with the design-token name it attributes that hex to, must equal the value that token resolves to in /home/user/circletel/tailwind.config.ts. Mechanically checkable: parse the `circleTel` and `ui` colour scales from tailwind.config.ts and diff against every (token, hex) pair asserted by the capability. Zero mismatches required.

DESIGN.md AGREEMENT — every colour and typeface this capability states for the web/product surface must equal the corresponding key in the `colors` and `typography` front-matter of /home/user/circletel/DESIGN.md. Mechanically checkable by parsing that YAML front-matter and diffing.

TYPEFACE AGREEMENT — the typefaces this capability names must be the typefaces production actually loads. Mechanically checkable: the `next/font/google` imports in /home/user/circletel/app/layout.tsx and the `fontFamily` map in tailwind.config.ts must contain every typeface the capability names, and the capability must name no typeface absent from both.

LOGO ARTWORK AGREEMENT — any hex the capability states as the logo's own orange or grey must match the dominant opaque pixel values of the artwork in .design/logos/. Mechanically checkable by sampling the PNGs. VERIFIED at synthesis time: LOGO-01 dominant opaque colours are #F6841F (orange, 611,179 px) and #757474 (grey, 309,010 px); LOGO-06 is #F6841F on white.
LOGO SET — exactly eight variants exist, stored as `.design/logos/FLAT COLOUR - CIRCLE TEL LOGO-0X.png` for X = 1..8. VERIFIED: all eight files present.
LOGO-01 — Orange + Grey on white/transparent. PRIMARY variant: website, documents, formal use, light backgrounds.
LOGO-02 — Orange only on white/transparent. Single-colour printing, embroidery.
LOGO-03 — Grey only on white/transparent. Neutral contexts, black-and-white documents.
LOGO-04 — Black only on white/transparent. High contrast, legal documents, stamps.
LOGO-05 — White only on transparent. Dark backgrounds (knocked out); also used over orange areas.
LOGO-06 — White mark on an orange background block. Social avatars, app icons, favicons; preferred when compositing onto dark or gradient backgrounds for high visibility.
LOGO-07 — Orange + Grey on white, small-size optimised. Email signatures, small placements.
LOGO-08 — Orange + Grey on white, large/high-resolution. Print, banners, billboards.

LOGO SELECTION — dark or black background → LOGO-05; social avatar or app icon → LOGO-06; print or large format → LOGO-08; email or small placement → LOGO-07; single-colour requirement → LOGO-02 (orange) or LOGO-03 (grey); formal, primary or default → LOGO-01. When compositing onto generated artwork specifically: dark or gradient background → LOGO-06; light or white background → LOGO-01; over orange areas → LOGO-05; print or large → LOGO-08; small or email → LOGO-07.

LOGO ANATOMY — dual swirl circles (outer orange, inner grey) signifying connectivity and dynamic service; a WiFi signal icon integrated with the letter 'c' signifying wireless/internet focus; wordmark 'circle' in lowercase orange followed by 'TEL' in uppercase bold grey. The artwork files are authoritative over any prose description of the mark.

WORDMARK CASING — the mark reads 'circle' lowercase + 'TEL' uppercase; this casing is part of the mark and must never be normalised to 'Circletel', 'CircleTEL' or 'CIRCLETEL' within the mark. In running prose the company name is written 'CircleTel'.
LOGO CLEARSPACE — padding equal to the height of the 'TEL' wordmark element, maintained on all four sides.
LOGO MINIMUM SIZE — 32px height for digital; 10mm height for print.
LOGO PROHIBITION — the logo is never generated, drawn or reconstructed by an image model in any medium; it is only ever composited or placed from the stored artwork files.

BRAND POSITIONING (DESIGN.md) — 'B2B/B2C ISP platform for South Africa. One Provider. One Bill. Your Office Runs.' Trusted connectivity for South African SMEs. Identity built on authority and warmth: the deep navy of a reliable enterprise partner, activated by a bold South African orange signalling energy and action. Design philosophy: professional-but-approachable; information-dense but calm; the interface should feel like a reliable local partner — knowledgeable, clear, always available.
MOOD AND AVOID-LIST — Style: modern, professional, South African market. Mood: trustworthy, innovative, approachable. Avoid: overly busy designs, neon colours, clip-art style.

ACCESSIBILITY INVARIANTS — decorative icons carry aria-hidden="true" with meaning conveyed by adjacent text; standalone meaningful icons and logos carry an accessible name; status is never communicated by colour alone; orange as text on white must be #AE5B16.

ICON SYSTEM — Phosphor via react-icons/pi for navigation, actions, status, controls and general interface symbols (prefer bold variants); Iconify via @iconify/react only for approved brand/provider/service/technology logos Phosphor lacks; neither library registered in globals.css. Production-critical icons hosted locally under components/icons/ (SVG-as-JSX) or public/icons/, preserving official geometry and colours, with the Iconify identifier, source URL, icon-set licence and attribution recorded in a source comment.

PRE-RELEASE VERIFICATION — before an asset is called done, confirm: the correct primary orange lineage was used for this destination; no off-brand colours are present; the logo variant suits its background; clearspace and minimum size are respected; the aesthetic is clean and professional; the depiction is South African market appropriate; the aspect ratio matches the destination; and the file is saved to the correct location. Where colour fidelity is load-bearing, this check must sample the rendered pixels against the approved hex rather than being made by eye.

contested_facts.assessed_authoritative: SPLIT AND UNRESOLVED BY EVIDENCE — this is a genuine two-lineage situation, not simple staleness, and it is escalated to the user. On the evidence: #E87A1E is authoritative for the web and product UI; the logo's own #F6841F (of which the skill's #F5831F is a faithful transcription) is authoritative for the mark itself and therefore constrains anything the mark sits on. #F59E0B and #F5841E are defects to be removed.
contested_facts.reasoning: Extractors 1 and 2 concluded #E87A1E simply wins on usage count and on the config's 'updated from wireframe spec' migration comment. I verified those counts (2,743 token uses vs 200 literals) and they hold — but that analysis is incomplete, because none of the extractors sampled the artwork. The logo PNGs are painted #F6841F. That is decisive new evidence: the skill's #F5831F is not a stale guess, it is the trademark's own colour transcribed to within one unit per channel, and #E87A1E is a later, darker web-UI value that the mark itself never adopted. This produces a concrete, visible defect that neither lineage's advocates have addressed: composite the real LOGO-01 onto a background painted circleTel-orange and two perceptibly different oranges appear in the same frame. So neither 'the skill is stale, use #E87A1E everywhere' nor 'the skill is right, ignore the tokens' is safe. Whether the marketing and UI oranges are deliberately different is a business decision, not one I can settle from the repository — nothing in DESIGN.md, tailwind.config.ts or the skill states an intended split. Escalated.

scope_in: Answering any question about CircleTel's own colours, typography, logo, clearspace, minimum sizes, wordmark casing, tone, positioning and market context.
Being the referenced source for those facts across every consumer — image generation, web and admin UI code, print, email, social, collateral, decks and product documentation.
Selecting the correct logo variant for a given background, medium and size, and stating why.
Supplying brand values in the form each consumer needs: exact hex for prompts, token names for code, RGB and millimetre values for print.
Supplying the brand context block and colour discipline that generative image consumers must inject, including the anti-drift qualifier where a model is known to shift the hue.
The rule and the operative defaults for compositing the real logo onto generated imagery rather than generating it.
Setting aspect ratio and resolution expectations per destination.
Governing where brand assets and prompt definitions are stored so they remain findable and reusable.
Stating the brand's accessibility floor for colour and icon usage, including which orange may carry text.
Validating a finished asset or rendered interface against the brand definition before release, and stating which brand decisions were applied.
Deriving a defensible answer, clearly labelled as a derivation, for a brand decision the definition does not cover.
Reporting conflicts between the repository's brand sources when a requested fact is contested.
scope_out: The mechanics of any specific image-generation provider — model names, API calls, pricing, CLI flags, retry behaviour. Those capabilities consume the brand; they are not it.
Creative direction, composition, lighting, camera specification, scene invention and prompt-engineering craft — these belong to the per-asset generation capabilities.

Web/UI SYSTEM facts that only screens use: grid, spacing rhythm, breakpoints, elevation levels, component anatomy, radii. DESIGN.md owns these. (They overlap with this capability only on colour and type — which is exactly where they currently disagree and must be reconciled rather than duplicated.)
Implementing components in React/Tailwind. The brand supplies the values, not the code.
Copywriting, messaging strategy, campaign concepting, offer construction, pricing decisions and claim substantiation.

Redesigning the brand — proposing new logo lockups, inventing new brand colours, or editing/re-exporting the authoritative logo source files. This capability reports and applies the brand; a change to a hex, typeface or logo is decided outside it and then recorded in it.
Third-party and partner brand identities beyond the rule that licence and trademark status must be checked before use.
Choosing or authoring interface icons beyond deferring to the established Phosphor/Iconify system.
General UI/UX quality, usability heuristics, conversion optimisation and layout critique beyond what the brand itself fixes.
Media buying, channel strategy, placement and platform publishing.
Legal clearance of trademarks, model releases and third-party imagery rights — escalated, not assumed.
Document and collateral templating and the confidentiality rules that govern them.
scope_verdict: THE AUTHORITATIVE BRAND DEFINITION, of which image generation is one consumer — not 'brand rules for image generation'. Four pieces of evidence decide it. (1) The dependency graph already contradicts the narrow framing: three non-image skills declare `dependencies: brand-design` — product-page-builder (code/UI), promotional-campaigns (marketing), new-product (product documentation) — so the demand is demonstrably broader than the framing it was given. (2) The narrow framing has demonstrably failed at its own job: six sibling image-generation skills each restate the brand block inline and none of them loads this skill, and they have already diverged from it (they adopted DESIGN.md's navy while keeping the skill's orange — a hybrid no source authorises). Being 'the image-gen brand skill' did not make it the source image generation consults. (3) The same facts independently live in DESIGN.md, tailwind.config.ts and app/globals.css — consumers the narrow framing does not even acknowledge, and the ones that have drifted furthest from it. (4) The facts themselves are medium-independent: a hex, a typeface, the logo variant inventory, clearspace and minimum size govern a printed banner, an email signature and a React component exactly as much as a generated image. But the verdict carries a hard boundary in the opposite direction, because broadening invites absorbing all of DESIGN.md: this capability owns brand IDENTITY facts — colour, type, logo, tone, market — which every medium shares. DESIGN.md owns web/UI SYSTEM facts — grid, spacing, elevation, component anatomy, radii — which only screens use. They overlap on colour and type, which is precisely where they currently disagree; the fix is one reconciled definition that both reference, not a tenth copy.
activation_expectations: Fires automatically on any request that will produce a CircleTel-branded visual artefact — image, mockup, social post, hero, banner, icon, deck, page, component — without the user having to ask for brand rules.
Fires on questions about CircleTel's colours, hex values, typography, logo, clearspace or minimum sizes, whatever the medium of the eventual answer.
Fires when a consumer needs a brand value in a specific form: hex for a prompt, token name for code, RGB or millimetres for print.
Fires when a logo must be placed and a variant must be chosen, or when an asset is being validated before release.
Fires even on small, internal, draft, exploratory or urgent requests — 'quick' is not an exemption.

Does NOT fire for visual work that is not CircleTel-branded: a generic chart, a third-party mockup, a diagram, a competitor screenshot. Over-application on keywords like 'design', 'colours' or 'image' is a real failure mode, not a safe default.
When it fires it must state the brand decisions it applied, so the user can see and correct them.
When a requested fact is contested it must say so and present the competing values with their sources, rather than answering as if settled.
non_qualities: Exhaustiveness of the palette — a short list of correct, role-tagged values beats a long swatch catalogue.
Prose quality, document structure, section ordering and table formatting.
Prompt-template wording and YAML framing — the phrasing is a convenience, the brand facts inside it are the substance.
Which image-generation model, provider or CLI is used, and its flags, pricing and output format.
The specific compositing implementation (library, script, code sample) — only the resulting placement, sizing, alpha preservation and quality matter.
Novelty or creative flair in the brand guidance itself; this capability is a reference, not a design exercise.
Speed of answering — a fast wrong hex is the failure this exists to prevent.
Backwards compatibility with the skill's own historical values where they contradict verified production tokens.
Visual distinctiveness of individual assets — real, but owned by the per-asset generation capabilities; brand compliance and distinctiveness are separate requirements.
Coverage of web layout, spacing, elevation and component anatomy — deliberately ceded to DESIGN.md.

unresolved_or_decided.issue: Scope: 'brand rules for image generation' versus 'the authoritative brand definition'
unresolved_or_decided.extractors_disagreed: Extractor_1 and extractor_3 both framed the capability around image generation, treating web/UI implementation as explicitly out of scope. Extractor_2 argued the image-generation framing is itself a means, not an end, and that the capability is the brand definition with a generation-facing view.
unresolved_or_decided.decision: Extractor_2's framing adopted, with a hard boundary at brand identity versus web/UI system facts. Recorded in full in scope_verdict.
unresolved_or_decided.reasoning: Extractor_2's evidence is the only evidence anyone offered on the question, and I verified and extended it: three non-image skills declare a dependency on brand-design, six image skills restate the brand inline and load none of it, and the same facts live in DESIGN.md, tailwind.config.ts and globals.css. Extractors 1 and 3 inherited the framing from the skill's own title rather than testing it. The boundary matters as much as the verdict — without it the capability swallows DESIGN.md's grid, spacing and elevation specs, which is the opposite failure.

unresolved_or_decided.issue: Whether to hardcode a primary orange hex in objective_invariants
unresolved_or_decided.extractors_disagreed: Extractor_3 asserted '#F5831F is exactly the primary orange' as a flat invariant. Extractor_1 recorded #F5831F as the invariant with a contested note attached. Extractor_2 declined to state a single value and recorded both lineages side by side.
unresolved_or_decided.decision: No orange hex is asserted as an invariant. The invariant is the mechanically checkable relation — the values stated must equal the values the production design tokens define, and any hex attributed to the logo must match the artwork pixels. The competing values are recorded in contested_facts with their evidence, and the business question is escalated.
unresolved_or_decided.reasoning: The brief is explicit on this and it is also correct: I cannot justify a hex I have not been authorised to choose. Extractor_3's flat assertion would bake a contested marketing value into a contract as fact. Extractor_1's asterisked invariant is self-undermining — an invariant with a 'this may be wrong' note attached is not an invariant. Extractor_2's abstention is closest to right but leaves nothing checkable. Framing it as an agreement relation gives a test that passes or fails today, survives whichever way the user settles the orange, and would have caught the drift years ago.

unresolved_or_decided.extractors_disagreed: Extractors 1 and 2 both concluded production supports #E87A1E and that the skill's #F5831F is stale legacy — extractor_1 called it a failure of the capability, extractor_2 allowed it might be a deliberate marketing lineage but found nothing supporting that. Extractor_3 declined to rank them and said the ambiguity must not be inherited.
unresolved_or_decided.decision: Rejected the 'simply stale' reading. Recorded as a genuine two-lineage split and escalated to the user, with the boundary question stated explicitly.
unresolved_or_decided.reasoning: None of the three extractors sampled the logo artwork. I did: LOGO-01 and LOGO-06 are painted #F6841F, within one unit per channel of the skill's #F5831F and visibly distinct from #E87A1E. That reframes the whole conflict — #F5831F is not drift, it is the trademark's own colour transcribed, and #E87A1E is a later web-UI value the mark never adopted. It also surfaces a concrete defect nobody had identified: compositing the real logo onto a circleTel-orange background puts two different oranges in one frame. Deciding for #E87A1E on usage count alone, as the majority reading would have, would have silently sanctioned that.

unresolved_or_decided.issue: Ranking of factual exactness versus logo integrity
unresolved_or_decided.extractors_disagreed: Extractors 1 and 2 ranked factual exactness first and logo integrity second and fourth respectively. Extractor_3 ranked logo integrity first, on the grounds that a hallucinated mark makes an asset unusable while a wrong hex is degradation.
unresolved_or_decided.reasoning: Extractor_3's argument about severity-per-instance is sound but addresses the wrong axis. Logo integrity is a single rule that is currently stated clearly and correctly and is demonstrably being followed — the '-bg' / '-composite' / '-final' filenames across two real campaigns prove it. Factual exactness is the axis on which the capability is failing right now, on six separate facts, silently, into shipped code. The contract should rank by where the risk actually is. Logo integrity stays at 2 because it is the one rule whose violation is unrecoverable, and because the six sibling image skills DO violate it.

unresolved_or_decided.issue: Status of the Tailwind token names
unresolved_or_decided.extractors_disagreed: Extractor_3 classified the token names as means and dropped them as 'demonstrably stale'. Extractor_2 kept them as an end whose specific mapping needs correcting. Extractor_1 recorded the skill's token names inside the invariants without separating name from value.

unresolved_or_decided.reasoning: Dropping the token column would remove the only mechanism by which a code consumer can be brand-correct without transcribing hexes, and transcription is exactly where drift enters. The token names are not stale — they are live and correct in the config; what is stale is the skill's claim about what they hold. Fixing the claim is the cheap correct move; deleting the column is throwing away the bridge because the sign on it was wrong.

unresolved_or_decided.extractors_disagreed: Extractor_3 treated contrast as a first-class gap with computed ratios. Extractor_2 made accessibility a brand constraint. Extractor_1 listed accessibility contrast auditing as explicitly out of scope.

unresolved_or_decided.extractors_disagreed: Extractor_1 checked it against tailwind, found the hex matched, and recorded 'no conflict'. Extractor_3 noticed it lives under a non-CircleTel namespace and called its brand status genuinely unclear.

unresolved_or_decided.issue: Depth of gap analysis to carry forward
unresolved_or_decided.extractors_disagreed: Extractor_3 enumerated eighteen gaps (dark mode, co-branding lockups, print CMYK/Pantone, gradient specification, favicon safe areas, SA legal guardrails, generated in-image claims, logo on noisy backgrounds, and more). The split is by whether the answer is derivable from existing facts or requires a brand-owner decision.

open_questions_for_user: PRIMARY ORANGE — is the split deliberate? The logo artwork is painted #F6841F (the skill's #F5831F is a faithful transcription of it), while the web UI token circleTel-orange is #E87A1E across 2,743 usages. Are these two intentionally different — a warmer marketing/imagery orange matching the mark, and a slightly deeper UI orange — or is one of them an accident that should be retired? If the split is deliberate, where exactly is the boundary: does an emailed PDF one-pager use the marketing orange or the UI orange? A slide deck? A product-page hero image that a React page renders beside a circleTel-orange button? Leaving this ambiguous is worse than either answer.

ORANGE COLLISION ON COMPOSITED ASSETS — when the real logo (#F6841F) is composited onto artwork painted in the UI orange (#E87A1E), two perceptibly different oranges appear in the same frame. Is that acceptable, or must generated backgrounds adopt the logo's orange whenever the mark will sit on them?

THE THIRD ORANGE — app/globals.css defines the shadcn --primary as oklch(0.7686 0.1647 70.0804), roughly #F59E0B, a generic amber, in both light and dark themes. Every unstyled shadcn primitive renders in it. Should this be corrected to whichever orange wins, or is it deliberately left as a neutral default?

ACCESSIBILITY FLOOR FOR MARKETING IMAGERY — the web UI is bound by WCAG AA and uses #AE5B16 for orange text on white. Neither candidate primary orange passes as text on white (2.58:1 and 2.90:1), and white text fails on either orange fill. Is marketing and social imagery held to the same floor, or is it explicitly exempt as non-interactive content? If exempt, does the exemption cover in-image pricing and offer text that customers must actually read?

AUTHORITY ORDER — when this capability, DESIGN.md and tailwind.config.ts disagree in future, which wins, and who is entitled to change a brand hex or typeface? Right now there is no stated precedence, which is how six facts drifted without anyone noticing.

PROPAGATION MODEL — six sibling image-generation skills each carry their own copy of the brand block and load none of this capability; three other skills declare a dependency on it. Should the copies be deleted and replaced with a reference, or is duplication accepted and periodically reconciled? Correcting the values here without settling this guarantees they are stale again within months.

LEGACY TOKEN RETIREMENT — circleTel-darkNeutral (#1F2937) has zero usages and can be retired outright. circleTel-lightNeutral (#E6E9EF) has 164 usages and cannot be removed without touching them. Should lightNeutral be migrated to an approved token, or kept as a sanctioned card/section tint?

SELECTED-STATE BLUE — #1E4B85 is used for selected package cards but is defined under a 'WebAfrica-inspired' namespace rather than the CircleTel palette. Is it a CircleTel brand colour, a tolerated UI state colour, or something to be replaced with navy?

TYPOGRAPHY IN GENERATED IMAGERY — production ships Manrope and Inter, but every image-generation path names no typeface at all, so generated assets carry no guarantee of matching the website. Should generated imagery specify Manrope and Inter by name, or is generic sans-serif acceptable in imagery on the grounds that models cannot honour a typeface reliably?

PRINT REPRODUCTION — logo variants exist explicitly for embroidery (02) and billboards (08), but no CMYK or Pantone equivalent for the orange is defined anywhere, nor a minimum print resolution or a rule for uncoated stock and garments. What are the approved print equivalents?

DARK MODE — the palette has no dark-surface tokens, no dark-mode orange treatment (saturated orange on near-black vibrates), and no rule for which logo variant applies in a dark UI theme as distinct from a dark photograph. Is dark mode in the brand's scope, and if so what are the values?

CO-BRANDING AND PARTNER LOCKUPS — CircleTel sells wholesale and partner-sourced services, so joint assets are inevitable, but there are no rules for relative mark sizing, separator treatment, order, clearspace between marks, or whether the orange-square lockup may appear in a lockup at all.
